evidence_set: The authors use receptor availability (non-displaceable binding potential), an indirect measure, instead of 'occupancy', which they call misleading and not measurable directly in people except with extraordinary methods (to obtain receptor concentration and affinity); if receptor affinity and endogenous opioid levels are assumed constant, a fall in availability is proportional to a rise in occupancy. Measures taken 4 hours after the daily dose, the earliest post-dose time studied, probably reflect less than the largest fall in availability; within-day PET time courses are not feasible. There is no gold-standard definition of clinically meaningful blockade, and neither the availability needed for withdrawal suppression or blockade nor how it varies with patients, opioids and routes is known.

The studies reviewed enrolled people dependent on heroin who were not seeking treatment and who usually kept using between inpatient stays; the authors call generalizability to people dependent on other opioids, such as oxycodone or hydrocodone, or seeking treatment unclear. Ages were limited to 18–50; many fewer women than men took part, and the small samples gave too little statistical power to examine gender or age; people with substance use disorders other than nicotine, depressive, psychotic or anxiety disorders, pregnancy or medical conditions such as active hepatitis were excluded, and the authors say these relatively healthy volunteers do not represent patients in clinical practice. All imaging used a buprenorphine-only product; the authors cite data suggesting that buprenorphine and buprenorphine/naloxone products under the tongue have similar effects.

evidence_set: The authors lack longitudinal follow-up of people with these lesions: only one included series (Trimarchi et al., 2003) gives some sparse information on progression over time, which they say seems to confirm their hypothesis; the order of spread (septum, then the lower third, then the middle third, then the skull base or lamina papyracea) is a hypothesis drawn from the decreasing counts, which needs prospective validation; one-sided use, septal deviation before use and the effect of substances mixed into cocaine could not be accounted for. The authors suggest that the lack of follow-up may be partly due to stigmatization (people with these lesions tend to seek care late and often perceive a request to stop cocaine as a moral judgment, citing one paper), which they say correlates with a high rate of loss to follow-up. The conclusion calls for prospective studies following the evolution of the lesions. Table 3 gives no use status for the 2003 series.

External nose involvement was listed for 10 of 17 series: saddle nose in 7 people across 5 series, collapse of the nasal pyramid in 7 people across the 2 series by Colletti et al. (whose durations of use, 5, 9, 10 and 10 years, and use status are identical in Table 3, so they may share patients), a nasal ala fistula with collapse of the dorsum-ala complex in 1 further person in one of those series (Colletti et al., 2014), single cases of destroyed nostrils, destroyed nasal ala and destroyed columella, columella and philtrum destruction in 1 of the saddle-nose cases, and 2 unspecified deformities (editors' count from Table 5). Few series gave solid data, and the authors say their analysis seems to suggest that no relationship can be drawn between the lesions inside the nose and the extent of external nose involvement.

evidence_set: Amphetamine screens: the energy supplement DMAA gave false positives on two laboratory assays, in spiked urine and in the urine of people taking it; three women prescribed labetalol screened positive and GC-MS found no amphetamines; metformin in a case report (one point-of-care test); promethazine (3 specimens) and chlorpromazine (6) were positive on one assay and negative by LC-PDA, and on retesting all 9 were negative on two other kits while 2 were positive on a third; trazodone added to drug-free urine gave false positives on one ecstasy (MDMA) screen but not on the same maker's amphetamine kit, which that study's authors think most likely due to its metabolite m-CPP; m-CPP gave false positives on another amphetamine assay (trazodone itself only above 200 µg/mL), on which 3 of 6 patients taking trazodone screened positive and were negative by GC-MS; in 6 healthy men given two doses of the antibiotic ofloxacin 12 hours apart, no sample before and all 6 samples after screened positive on one amphetamine assay, the lowest almost four times the 300 ng/mL cutoff.

In a retrospective chart review of amphetamine screens (Syva EMIT II Plus) that GC-MS did not confirm, 41% of the samples (printed in words; 53 patients) came from patients taking bupropion at the time; after statistically ruling out polysubstance use as a cause, the investigators are said to have concluded that a large portion of these false positives stemmed directly from bupropion; no spiking experiment showed that bupropion or its metabolites caused the result, which the authors call an important limitation. The total number of unconfirmed screens and the share of people taking bupropion who screened positive are not given. Editors' arithmetic: about 129 unconfirmed screens if 53 is 41%.

Cannabis (THC) screens: urine of patients taking efavirenz screened positive on three immunoassays (cutoff 50 µg/L), an interference attributed to its glucuronide metabolite (efavirenz and 8-OH efavirenz were found not to interfere); in another study, Rapid Response test strips were positive in 28 of 30 patients taking efavirenz for at least 2 weeks, while the other point-of-care device and two automated immunoassays were negative; in 5 volunteers taking the anti-inflammatory niflumic acid, all 55 urine samples were positive on Roche KIMS and negative on Syva EMIT; four commercial baby soaps gave positives on the Vitros THC immunoassay at a 20 ng/mL cutoff; ibuprofen and naproxen are listed as case reports with the Syva EMIT d.a.u. cannabinoid assay (cutoff 20 µg/L) and with the Abbott TDx barbiturate assay (Table VI).

PCP screens: because PCP use is rare and PCP immunoassays are not specific, the positive predictive value of a PCP screen is very low. Venlafaxine: after an overdose, one assay was positive for PCP and GC-MS negative; in three other patients taking venlafaxine, one point-of-care test was positive at a 25 ng/mL cutoff while three other PCP assays and GC-MS were negative. Tramadol: false positives with negative GC-MS in two patients who had taken large overdoses (one assay), with tramadol and N-desmethyltramadol each triggering that assay in spiked urine, and in two further overdose patients on another assay. MDPV ('bath salts') in spiked urine gave false-positive PCP results on one assay, after a patient's apparent overdose with no PCP found; lamotrigine in a case report. LSD screens cross-reacted with many medicines on one assay (EMIT II LSD), among them amitriptyline, bupropion, fluoxetine, haloperidol, risperidone, sertraline and trazodone; the mucus-thinning medicine ambroxol caused unexpected LSD positives in twelve patients (the review does not name the assay) and also cross-reacts significantly with the CEDIA DAU LSD assay (spiked urine in Table VI).

evidence_set: Efficacy is reported only as parents' global ratings, 86 of 125 (68.8%) rated improved on dexamphetamine and 90 (72%) on methylphenidate, not tested against each other, with a statement without figures that teacher and parent Conners ratings generally agreed with these proportions. For complaints that fell on medicine, the authors offer three explanations: parents' over-reporting before diagnosis, the complaints being features of ADHD itself that lessen with treatment (the reading their conclusions adopt), and mothers' changed view of the child. They note, citing a placebo-controlled trial, that comparison with baseline may understate a drug's adverse effects, adding that this would not affect the comparison of the two drugs; ratings were mostly in the mild range of the 0 to 9 scale; and only moderate doses given twice a day were studied, so other doses and spacing might give different side-effect profiles.

evidence_set: Table 3, stated to be modified from the author's own 1998 paper, lists eight single-dose study arms of a benzodiazepine with alcohol: benzodiazepine metabolism 'unchanged' in five (alprazolam 0.5 and 2 mg by mouth with ethanol 0.8 g/kg, by plasma concentration; diazepam 5 mg with 48 g; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg drunk 3 hours after the diazepam; diazepam 10 mg with an intravenous ethanol infusion; triazolam 0.5 mg with 25 g), 'decreased' in two (brotizolam 0.25 mg with 24 g: Cmax, half-life and clearance; diazepam 10 mg with 0.8 g/kg: plasma concentration) and 'increased' in one (triazolam 0.5 mg with an ethanol 'loading' regimen, which the footnote, ambiguously worded, describes as oral ethanol for 7.5 hours starting 1 hour before, holding breath concentrations at 800–950 mg/L: area under the curve, mean 21%); doses are the studies' conditions. The column is headed 'Benzodiazepine Metabolism' with the measure in brackets, so for the three changed arms it is not stated whether the word refers to metabolism or to the measure. The abstract says that metabolism is in general delayed with acute alcohol, although some reports suggest otherwise; the text cites an older review (Sellers and Busto, 1982) as finding benzodiazepine concentrations raised in most cases.

Table 4 lists fatal poisonings with both ethanol and benzodiazepines in the blood, described as cases reported from 1988 to the present, with no total and no count of people who took both and lived. Editors' count of the rows: 39 deaths from 10 reports (references 49–58, published 1988–1999), 25 of them from one Canadian forensic series of triazolam cases (Joynt, 1993; footnoted as covering only deaths due to drugs and drug-related deaths); 32 rows name triazolam; blood ethanol 0.1–3.2 mg/mL (editors' median 1.7); triazolam at or below 20 ng/mL, the top of the therapeutic range the table quotes from one case report (reference 55), in 13 of the 32, counting one trace; alprazolam in 3 rows, each with other substances (200 ng/mL with triazolam and others; a trace with triazolam, diazepam and nordiazepam; 210 ng/mL with others, in a report titled as a fatal overdose of tramadol and alprazolam). The text states, without a count, that fatal poisoning appears to occur more often with ethanol and several benzodiazepines than with one, adding that an excess total amount of benzodiazepines must also be considered, and puts the many triazolam reports down, probably, to its lower therapeutic concentration.
